# Finding and Fixing Errors in Visual Studio
## Error Indicators in the Editor
Visual Studio checks your code as you type and marks problems with colored squiggly lines.
Squiggle Meaning
Red An error, so the code cannot be compiled and the program cannot run
Green A warning, so the program still runs but something may be wrong
A common warning is a variable that is declared but never used. Hovering over a squiggly line shows a description of the problem and any quick fixes. Many code editors mark errors this way.
## The Error List Window
The Error List collects every error and warning in one place. It can be opened from the View menu, or from the Error List tab at the bottom of the window. Double-clicking an error or warning jumps to the exact line in the code. It is a good habit to keep the Error List open while coding, so problems are easy to see.
## Running Code with Errors
A program with errors cannot be run. When Start is pressed, Visual Studio shows a message that there were build errors and asks whether to run the last successful build. Choose No. Choosing Yes runs the last version that worked, which does not include the new code.
## Reading Error Messages
Error messages are written in plain English, so reading them carefully usually shows what to fix.
Message Usual Cause
; expected A semicolon is missing at the end of a statement
The name does not exist in the current context A name is misspelled, has the wrong capitalization, or is used outside its scope
Use of unassigned local variable A variable is used before it has been given a value

C# → Basics → Fundamentals → Variables and Data Types (Declaring a Variable)
## Summary
  • Red squiggles are errors, and green squiggles are warnings.
  • The Error List shows every problem, and double-clicking one jumps to it.
  • When asked to run the last successful build after an error, choose No.

# How Visual Studio Helps You Write Code
## What IntelliSense Is
IntelliSense is the box of suggestions that pops up while you type. It helps you write code faster and with fewer typing mistakes.
## Completing a Name
Typing part of a name, such as Con, shows a list of matching names.
1. **Move to the suggestion**
  • Use the arrow keys to highlight Console in the list.
2. **Press Tab**
  • Visual Studio completes the full name.
Completing a name also fixes its capitalization. Typing console with a lowercase c and pressing Tab changes it to Console.
See: C# → Basics → Fundamentals → Syntax & Structure (Case Sensitivity)
## Members After the Dot
Typing a dot after a name, such as Console., opens a list of everything inside it. This list shows the methods and properties that can be used. Selecting a name shows a short description of what it does.
See: C# → Basics → Core Concepts → Operators (Dot Operator)
## Parameter Info and Overloads
Opening the parentheses after a method, such as Console.WriteLine(, shows what the method accepts. Many methods can be called in several ways, and each way is called an overload. A count in the pop-up shows which overload is displayed, and the up and down arrow keys move through them. Browsing the overloads shows what kind of value a method accepts, such as a string for text.
## Summary
  • IntelliSense suggests names as you type, and the arrow keys and Tab complete them.
  • Typing a dot lists the members of a class or object.
  • Opening parentheses shows the overloads a method accepts.

# Your First C# Project in Visual Studio
## Creating a New Project
Steps to start a new C# project:
1. **Open Visual Studio**
  • Start from the start window.
2. **Choose Create a new project**
  • This opens the list of project templates.
3. **Choose Console App**
  • Pick the C# Console App template for basic applications.
  • Other C# project templates are available for other kinds of applications.
4. **Name the project**
  • Click Next, then enter the project name and location.
5. **Choose the .NET version**
  • Click Next to reach the Additional information page.
  • Choose the latest LTS version if possible.
6. **Click Create**
  • Visual Studio generates a starter project with a code file ready for editing.
## The Starter Code
The current Console App template generates top-level statements. The compiler creates the class and the Main method behind the scenes. ```csharp // See https://aka.ms/new-console-template for more information Console.WriteLine("Hello, World!"); ``` Older templates, including .NET Framework projects, generate the full structure instead. ```csharp using System; namespace MyProject { class Program { static void Main(string[] args) { } } } ``` The Additional information page also has a Do not use top-level statements check box. Checking it generates the full structure with an explicit Main method.
See: C# → Basics → Fundamentals → Syntax & Structure (Entry Point and the Main Method)
## Running the Project
Both run commands are in the Debug menu.
Command Shortcut
Start Debugging F5
Start Without Debugging Ctrl + F5
Start Debugging runs the program with the debugger attached, so breakpoints can pause it. Start Without Debugging runs the program without the debugger. The green Start button in the toolbar runs the program the same way as F5. The first run takes longer than later runs, because the project has to be compiled first.
## When the Console Window Closes Immediately
A console program closes its window as soon as it finishes running. In .NET Framework projects, starting with F5 closes the window immediately, so the output cannot be read. There are a few ways to keep the window open:
  • Run with Ctrl + F5, which keeps the window open and shows a Press any key to continue message.
  • Add Console.ReadLine() to the end of the code, which pauses the program until Enter is pressed.
In current .NET projects, Visual Studio keeps the console open by default after the program ends. This is controlled by the Automatically close the console when debugging stops option under Tools, Options, Debugging, General.
See: C# → Basics → Core Concepts → Console (Console.ReadLine)
## Running the Wrong Project
If a solution has more than one project, the Start button only runs the startup project. When the output is not what the code should produce, check which project is set as the startup project.
See: Visual Studio → Advanced → Workflow & Shortcuts → Startup Projects & Multi-Project Solutions
## Summary
  • A Console App project is created from the start window, and the template sets up the starter code.
  • F5 starts with debugging, and Ctrl + F5 starts without it.
  • Ctrl + F5 keeps the console window open after the program finishes.

# Finding Your Way Around a Visual Studio Solution
## What Solution Explorer Shows
Solution Explorer lists every project in the solution, along with the files inside each project. It works like a folder that holds all of your work. The structure it shows matches the folders on disk, so a project folder in Solution Explorer is a project folder in the file system. If Solution Explorer is not visible, open it from the View menu.
## Solutions and Projects
Term Meaning
Solution The container that holds one or more projects, saved in a .sln file
Project A single program or library with its own code files
## Adding a Project to a Solution
1. **Right-click the solution**
  • Right-click the solution at the top of Solution Explorer.
2. **Add a new project**
  • Choose Add, then New Project.
3. **Choose the template and name**
  • Pick a template such as Console App and give the project a name.
Both projects now appear in Solution Explorer. Pressing Start only runs one of them, the startup project.
See: Visual Studio → Advanced → Workflow & Shortcuts → Startup Projects & Multi-Project Solutions
## Adding a File to a Project
1. **Right-click the project or a folder**
  • Right-click it in Solution Explorer.
2. **Choose Add, then New Item**
  • The Add New Item window opens.
3. **Choose Class**
  • A class creates a .cs file.
4. **Name it and click Add**
  • For example, name the file Player.cs.
The shortcut for Add New Item is Ctrl + Shift + A. Adding files through Solution Explorer keeps larger projects organized.
## Reopening a Solution
A closed solution can be opened again in two ways:
  • Choose it from the recent list in Visual Studio.
  • Double-click the .sln file in the solution folder.
## Summary
  • Solution Explorer shows all projects and files, matching the folders on disk.
  • A solution can hold several projects.
